title: Attributing a Campaign Without Mistakes
context: A campaign targets your organization: deceptive emails, custom tools, persistence, and collection of research documents. Management wants to know "who".

n1.text: Which element do you start profiling with?

choices.text: Observed techniques and attributes: access, resources, sophistication
choices.why: Profiling relies on behavioral and technical indicators, not intuition.

choices.text: The name of a known group mentioned in an article
choices.why: Group names are out of scope and tools are shared.

choices.text: The IP address of the phishing server
choices.why: An isolated IOC is not enough to classify an actor.

n2.text: The attackers target trade secrets with custom tools and a multi-month campaign. Which category is most likely?

choices.why: The sophistication and duration rule out an opportunist.

choices.text: State-sponsored actor or competitor, motivated by espionage / intellectual property
choices.why: Resources, sophistication, and motivation converge toward espionage.
A hacktivist primarily seeks visibility, not quiet theft of research.

n3.text: How do you present this conclusion to management?

choices.text: With a confidence level and the list of indicators, remaining ready to reassess
choices.why: Attribution is probabilistic: it is expressed with a confidence level and evolves with evidence.
Certain attribution based on partial indicators is a classic mistake.

choices.text: Say nothing, because attribution has no operational value
choices.why: The profile guides prioritization and which controls to strengthen.

n4.outcome: You profiled techniques and attributes, identified a consistent motivation, and expressed cautious attribution.

debrief: Classify the actor by motivation and attributes, not by the tool used.
Internal/external, resources, and sophistication are the three official axes.
Attribution is expressed with a confidence level and can be reassessed.
